topics.title: A one-act comic play: how plays work

learn.hook: A man comes to propose marriage, but ends up fighting about a meadow and a dog. Only on stage!
points: 'The Proposal' by Anton Chekhov is a one-act comic play: Lomov visits his neighbour Chubukov to propose to his daughter Natalya.
Before he can propose, Lomov and Natalya quarrel about the Oxen Meadows, and later about whose dog is better. They get engaged, but keep quarrelling.
A one-act play is short, has one act, few characters and usually one setting.
A play is told through dialogue; stage directions (often in brackets or italics) tell actors how to move and speak.
A farce is a comedy built on exaggerated characters and silly situations.

example.q: Scene: RAHUL (nervously): Uncle, I have come to ask... to ask... / MR VERMA (smiling): Speak up, beta! / RAHUL (clutching his chest): My heart is pounding! What do the words in brackets do?
steps: '(nervously)', '(smiling)', '(clutching his chest)' are not spoken aloud.
They tell the actor how to speak or what to do.
example.answer: They are stage directions: they show how the characters speak and act.

learn.reallife: School annual-day plays, street plays (nukkad natak) and TV sitcoms all use dialogue and stage directions.

games.title: Play check
items: 'The Proposal' is a one-act play.
It is a short comedy in one act.
Stage directions are spoken aloud by the actors.
They guide the actors and are not spoken.
Lomov and Natalya quarrel about the Oxen Meadows.
Each claims the meadows belong to their family.
Lomov goes to Chubukov's house to buy a dog.
He goes there to propose marriage to Natalya.
At the end, Lomov and Natalya stop quarrelling for ever.
They get engaged but begin to quarrel again.
A play tells its story mainly through dialogue.
Characters reveal the story by what they say and do.

quiz.q: Scene: RAHUL (nervously): Uncle, I have come to ask... to ask... / MR VERMA (smiling): Speak up, beta! / RAHUL (clutching his chest): My heart is pounding! What do the words in brackets tell us?
options: How the characters speak and act

quiz.q: In 'The Proposal', why does Lomov visit Chubukov's house?
quiz.explain: He arrives in formal dress to propose to Natalya.
quiz.mistake: Remembers the quarrels but not the purpose

quiz.q: What do Lomov and Natalya quarrel about first?
quiz.explain: The first quarrel is over who owns the Oxen Meadows; the dog quarrel comes later.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the two quarrels

quiz.q: What is the second big quarrel in 'The Proposal' about?
quiz.explain: Lomov's dog Guess and the Chubukovs' dog Squeezer are compared.

quiz.q: Scene: RAHUL (nervously): Uncle, I have come to ask... to ask... / MR VERMA (smiling): Speak up, beta! / RAHUL (clutching his chest): My heart is pounding! Report: Mr Verma said to Rahul, 'Speak up, beta!'
options: Mr Verma told Rahul speak up beta.
Mr Verma said Rahul that he speaks up.
Mr Verma told to Rahul speak up.
Mr Verma affectionately told Rahul to speak up.
quiz.explain: A command is reported with told + person + to + verb; 'beta' is replaced by 'affectionately'.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the form of address and the command form

teach.praise: Bravo-chirp! Plays use dialogue and stage directions to tell the story. Curtain up!
teach.nudge: How do characters tell the story in a play? And how do actors know what to do?

topics.title: Chekhov and comic characters: describing traits

learn.hook: A man who claims his heart is pounding and his leg is numb, every few minutes! Chekhov makes it hilarious.
points: Anton Chekhov (1860-1904) was a Russian writer of plays and short stories, and also a doctor.
In 'The Proposal', Lomov keeps complaining about his health: palpitations, a numb leg. He worries too much about illness.
The humour comes from exaggeration and irony: people meant to be planning a marriage quarrel over trifles.
Character-trait words: quarrelsome (likes to argue), hypochondriac (worries too much about health), irritable (easily annoyed), impulsive (acts without thinking).
Many adjectives come from nouns with suffixes: quarrel → quarrelsome, nerve → nervous, humour → humorous, anger → angry.

example.q: In the play, Lomov complains of palpitations and a numb foot every time Natalya disagrees with him about a small matter. What trait does this show, and why is it funny?
steps: He reacts to a small argument as if he is seriously ill.
That shows he worries too much about his health: a hypochondriac.
The gap between the tiny cause and his huge reaction is exaggeration, which makes us laugh.
example.answer: He is a hypochondriac; his huge reaction to a small quarrel is comic exaggeration.

learn.reallife: Comedians often exaggerate everyday habits, such as an uncle who checks the gas knob ten times before leaving.

quiz.explain: Chekhov was a Russian playwright and short-story writer.
quiz.mistake: Confuses him with Maupassant, who was French

quiz.q: Besides writing, what was Chekhov's profession?
quiz.explain: Chekhov trained and worked as a doctor.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a profession linked to the play's landowners

quiz.q: Chekhov is best known for which kinds of writing?
quiz.explain: He is famous for his plays and short stories.
quiz.mistake: Does not recall his literary forms

quiz.q: What does Lomov keep complaining about in 'The Proposal'?
options: His health, such as palpitations and a numb leg
quiz.explain: He keeps mentioning palpitations and other aches.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the running joke of the play

options: Someone who worries too much about their health
A doctor who treats the heart
quiz.explain: A hypochondriac fears being ill even without real cause.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the person with a doctor

quiz.explain: -some here means 'tending to': quarrelsome = tending to quarrel.

options: The characters quarrel over trifles instead of getting on with the proposal
quiz.explain: Exaggerated quarrels over small matters keep delaying the proposal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks humour must come from jokes or songs

quiz.q: Which is the adjective form of 'humour'?
quiz.explain: Humour + -ous gives 'humorous' (note the spelling drops the 'u').
quiz.mistake: Adds the wrong suffix or keeps 'humour' unchanged

teach.ask: Gappu: Why is the man in Chekhov's play so funny? He keeps saying his heart is bursting!
teach.praise: Ha-ha-chirp! He exaggerates and quarrels over small things. That's Chekhov's comedy!
teach.nudge: What does Lomov keep complaining about? And are the quarrels about big or small things?
